TP5: Hierarchical Model

Author

Lionel Hertzog

Published

August 17, 2026

1 Objectives

This practical aims at discovering hierarchical models, we will rely on the lme4 package to fit the models. The data used are flora species richness at NFI plots situated in different sylvoecoregions.

Remember the standard formula for a simple hierarchical model:

\[ \mu_{ij} = \beta_0 + \gamma_j + \beta_1 * X_i + ...\] \[ \gamma_j \sim N(0, \sigma_{hier})\]

With \(j\) a grouping index, in our case this will be the sylvoécoregions.

2 Read the data

Load the dat_tp5.csv into R. Perform quick exploration of the dataset.

here::i_am("practicals/tp5.qmd")
dat <- read.csv("../data/dat_tp5.csv")

head(dat)
      idp rich ser_86              pro_psg elev tcar esspre_fr
1 1005709   19    G11     privé - sans psg  319    1         R
2 1001933   50    C52     privé - sans psg  763    4         F
3 1001580   12    B33     privé - sans psg  206   10         F
4 1031119   26    I11     privé - sans psg  515   10         F
5 1007941   37    C20 publics - domaniales  465    8         F
6 1008363   35    F12 publics - domaniales  122    2         F

Metadata:

  • idp: plot id
  • rich: the number of flora species
  • ser_86: code id for the sylvoécoregion
  • pro_psg: ownerhip status of the plot
  • elev: the elevation in meter
  • tcar: the tree cover in percent
  • esspre_fr: whether the dominant tree species is deciduous (F) or confierous (R)
  • nb_tree: total number of trees in the plot

3 Fit a first non-hierarchical model

First fit a non-hierarchical model with (g)lm with the following formula:

rich ~ ser_86 + elev + tcar + pro_psg + esspre_fr

Choose an appropriate function between lm or glm with an appropriate distribution.

Look at the output of the model summary, what is the issue here? How would you solve this?

4 Fit a hierarchical model

4.1 Fit

Using lme4 fit the same model as before but putting the sylvoécoregions code as hierarchical term, in other words allowing for average richness to vary per regions. The main functions to fit these models are lmer for normal distribution and glmer for other distributions.

TipHint

A variable intercept hierarchical term, which is what we want here, can be coded in the model formula as:

lmer(y ~ ... + (1 | ser_86), ...)

The (1 | ser_86) synthax imply that the intercept (the 1) vary per ser_86 level.

4.2 Explore

  • Explore the output of the model, using the functions summary
  • Compare the standard deviation of the residuals with the standard deviation of the intercept, what do these quantities tell us? How large is the variation of the average richness per region compared to the residual variation?
  • The functions fixef and ranef allow to extract the estimated regression coefficients and the estimated average richness per regions. Write a couple of sentences about these estimations.

5 Interprete the covariables effects

5.1

Make plots of the estimated effects of the different covariables using ggeffets::predict_response, what do these results tell us?

5.2

In hierarchical models the explained variance (R-square) can be divided between the fixed covariables (here pro_psg, tcar …) and the hierarchical term (here the intercept varying between regions, also called the random part). Using the function rsq from the rsq package compute the R square from these different component and interpret the result.

6 Interprete the varying intercept

6.1

  • Make a plot of the estimated varying intercepts per sylvoecoregions together with the uncertainty.
  • Interpret the plot, what do the values mean and why are there negative values?
TipHint

The variance around the estimated varying intercepts are stored by default in the object returned by ranef.

ser_var <- ranef(m)
str(ser_var)
List of 1
 $ ser_86:'data.frame': 86 obs. of  1 variable:
  ..$ (Intercept): num [1:86] -5.29 -7.23 -8.62 -8.39 -7.27 ...
  ..- attr(*, "postVar")= num [1, 1, 1:86] 1.29 2.7 1.66 2.94 1.98 ...
 - attr(*, "class")= chr "ranef.mer"
TipSolution

Here is one way to bring this all in a tidy format and a plot option with gglot2.

ser_df <- data.frame(ser_86 = rownames(ser_var$ser_86),
                     ser_eff = ser_var$ser_86[,1],
                     ser_var = attr(ser_var$ser_86, "postVar")[,,1:86])
head(ser_df)
  ser_86   ser_eff  ser_var
1    A11 -5.291368 1.285263
2    A12 -7.232693 2.704827
3    A13 -8.619060 1.658244
4    A21 -8.394103 2.936493
5    A22 -7.274453 1.976975
6    A30 -5.396796 2.936493
library(tidyverse)
ggplot(ser_df, aes(x = fct_reorder(ser_86, ser_eff),
                   y = ser_eff, 
                   ymin = ser_eff - sqrt(ser_var),
                   ymax = ser_eff + sqrt(ser_var))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_linerange() +
  coord_flip()

6.2 Bonus

Make a plot of the relation between the estimated uncertainty for the regional variation in richness with the number of plots per regions. Does the plot seems logical to you?

6.3

The output of the ranef function are the deviation to the population-level intercept, negative values meaning lower richness values for the given region compared to the average. To get the predicted average richness level per region, the function ggeffects::predict_response(..., type = "random") can be used.

Plot the resulting estimation, compare to the deviations obtained via ranef.

7 Bonus: make a map

A shapefile of the sylvoécoregions is in the repository, make a map of the predicted average richness per regions.

TipHint

The sf package allows to manipulate spatial data in R, the function st_read reads in spatial data. The ggplot2 package also allows via geom_sf to plot sf objects.

TipSolution 
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
ser_shape <- st_read("../data/ser_27572.gpkg")
Reading layer `ser_27572' from data source 
  `D:\Documents\LIF\Enseignement\DAST\data\ser_27572.gpkg' using driver `GPKG'
Simple feature collection with 86 features and 2 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 47493 ymin: 1617395 xmax: 1197902 ymax: 2677441
Projected CRS: NTF (Paris) / Lambert zone II
ser_pred <- as.data.frame(ggeffects::predict_response(m, terms = "ser_86", type = "random"))
ser_plot <- inner_join(ser_pred, ser_shape, by = c("x" = "codeser"))

ggplot(ser_plot, aes(fill = predicted, geometry = geom)) +
  geom_sf() +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Greens", direction = -1) +
  theme_void()
